utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth; good morning, interpreters, registry staff, counsel for the Prosecution and the Defence; good morning, General Krstic. Before we resume, if I remember well, our next witness is Ms. Frease who should testify. We wish to tell the parties that the Judges have decided to authorise the Prosecutor to call an investigator to testify on the statements made in his presence by the person that you know and whose name I will not mention. This decision is without any prejudice to the final ruling that the Judges will render regarding the admission of the statements in question. The Judges expect the Prosecutor to provide all useful information regarding the actual presence of that investigator and the conditions under which the statements of the person concerned were taken. The Judges also require that the Prosecutor provide them, before calling the investigator, the written transcripts of those statements, whatever the form may be, and also that the Prosecutor have available the recordings of those statements, if any exist, so that the Chamber and the parties in the courtroom, that is, the Defence, may hear the parties regarding that recording. So the procedure will be that the witness will be in the courtroom, he will take the solemn declaration, we will hear the parties, upon which we will begin with the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination of that witness. That is the position of the Chamber. I see Mr. Visnjic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to provide an explanation in connection with a statement we made yesterday, so I would request that we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Stefanie Frease. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I need to raise my hand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Not necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Try and sit as comfortably as possible. I think you're used to being in a courtroom. You will now be answering questions put to you by Mr. Harmon, and then questions from the Defence counsel, and finally the Judges. Mr. Harmon, your witness. And thank you, Witness, for coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Frease. Could you state your full name and spell your last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. Stefanie May Frease, F-r-e-a-s-e.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell us your educational background?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I have a bachelor's degree from the University of Washington and a master's degree from Columbia University, both in international affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you ever given sworn testimony in a court of law?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, were you employed by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When were you employed by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I began working for the OTP April 26th, 1995, and worked for the OTP through July of 2000. I was then on a leave of absence and officially terminated my work with the Tribunal in December of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you came to work for the Office of the Prosecutor, were you assigned to work on the Srebrenica investigation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. It was roughly, I guess, three or four months after I arrived that I first became involved in the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Initially I was a part of a team that conducted an assessment mission to Bosnia, for about four weeks, and then I was formally assigned to the team in January of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have an understanding of the B/C/S language?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How would you rate your proficiency?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I would say that I'm highly proficient in the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Reading, writing, and speaking?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, at some point in time while you were a member of the team investigating the events in Srebrenica, did the Office of the Prosecutor acquire a large amount of data relating to radio intercepted communications?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And for want of a better term, were you involved in what came to be known as the Intercept Project?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could you tell the Judges what the Intercept Project was?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: The Intercept Project involved collecting material, assembling the material, and then beginning a process of analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, was the -- did the material come to the Office of the Prosecutor in the English language?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No, it didn't. It was all in the B/C/S language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there a large volume of this material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, and the volume increased over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you describe to the Trial Chamber your work in the Intercept Project, starting first of all with what your role was in it.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I was -- when we received the first material in, I believe it was March 1998, we received printouts, and after receiving that material I put together a small group of people to begin to go through the material and translate it. After that we began to enter the data into a very simple database, and after that we began to work on -- after we acquired the notebooks, then we began to enter the material from the notebooks also into this fairly simple database at that time and looked to cross-reference the material that we had received in written format with the material that we received in the notebooks. Then, of course, that also expanded to the tapes. So it was a constant process of cross-referencing all of the material that we received from -- first from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and then from the State Security Services of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you continue to work on analysing the intercepted radio communication material until you left the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I worked on it almost non-stop from March 1998 to early July 2000. There were a few months in there where I was assigned to other projects, but I always also kept abreast of what was going on in the project.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in the project, were you assisted by others?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Without naming the others, unless you're asked by either the Trial Chamber or Defence counsel, could you just describe what functions the other people had?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Sure. Initially, we worked with a small group. When we first received the printed material we worked with a small group of translators in the field, primarily, and then just to get a handle on what the information contained so that it could be shared with the team. Then when we started -- when we formed a very small group of people to work on this in-house, they -- I was assisted by language, people with language skills, only people who had language skills in the area, so interpreters and language assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you also at times assisted by the investigators themselves in attempting to locate persons or items that you deemed were important in continuing with your project?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, just to give the Judges a sense of dealing with this material, is it something that is requested be analysed very quickly and turned around or is it slow, laborious, time-consuming process? Can I get your comments and your views on that particular issue?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It was a much more laborious process than I think we had anticipated, and it was more laborious and took, really, quite a lot of time because of the various sources of the information, those being the printed material that we were first provided, then cross-referencing the printed material with the notebooks, and then working eventually with the tapes, so -- and simultaneously working on translations and also on developing a database which would allow us to conduct searches speedily so that we could make connections between conversations. I should mention that that was also another very big part of this project and something that required a lot of time and a lot of knowledge of the material, because we quickly started -- could begin -- we quickly started to see connections between various conversations, that we were -- that we weren't just dealing with one conversation, that we were getting two or three -- two or three conversations that were the same but that had been recorded by different operators.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, was one of your objectives in conducting the intercept project an attempt to determine whether this material was reliable and whether it was genuine?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In pursuing that objective, did you, among other things, attempt to locate, identify, and interview the intercept operators who allegedly had intercepted these communications?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, that came about a year into the project.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After some initial analysis, I take it, had been done?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, was there an attempt by you and the other people involved in the project to attempt to corroborate the contents of these intercepted communications?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in conducting your analysis and in attempting to determine whether these were genuine and reliable, could you tell the Judges what factors you considered in assessing the reliability of the material that you had received and were analysing?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Uh-huh. First we looked for internal consistency among the documents that we had been -- what we had received from the army and the police. And what I mean by "internal consistency" is that the printouts that we received matched verbatim with the notebooks that we received. So that was -- that was one part. That was sort of the preliminary part of testing the internal consistency. But also having a knowledge of the case more broadly, it was possible to know and to ascertain that what was contained within the intercepts was consistent with what we knew about the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you, for example, attempt to analyse materials that had come, that had been intercepted, from two different locations, Konjuh and Okresanica, to determine if at or about the same time a similar conversation had been intercepted?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that factor what led you believe that these were reliable?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. It certainly contributed greatly to the reliability when we learned that there were these two different sites and when we started to find examples of the same conversation. It wasn't immediately clear to us why we were finding similar conversations or really the same conversation with slight variations, and then understanding that there were two different sites and different units working, that contributed greatly to the sense that these were genuine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you also receive radio intercepted communication data from different sources, the army and the SDB?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you make a comparison of those two bodies of information? In other words, did you compare the intercepts of the SDB against the intercepts of the army in order to attempt to determine whether similar conversations were captured at the same time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We also did that kind of comparison. We -- really, what we used as the bases were the individual conversations. From those individual conversations, then we would cross-reference them with all of the other material. So all of the material that came from the Konjuh site, all of the material that came from the Okresanica site and all of the material that came from the police and created a database that allowed us to cross-reference all of these sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So that was a factor, I take it, when you found -- was that a factor -- strike that. Were your findings in relation to the consistencies between the two separate sources of intercept material a factor that led you to believe these were reliable?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, as a part of the exercise to determine whether or not these intercepts were reliable, did you then have interviewed the various intercept operators who had been identified?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you personally interview some of those operators?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And based on what they had informed you about, did that contribute at all to your analysis of whether these materials were genuine and reliable?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, it did. It did very much, because we had an opportunity to ask them about the process and to understand the process that they used in intercepting the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, as an additional measure of testing, I should say, these materials, did you at some point in time take a selection, small selection of these documents and attempt to verify the documents through third-party information, independent-party information?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Judges what that project entailed?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. While we were in the process of analysing the intercepts, when we came across information that appeared to be -- that appear as if we could corroborate it independently, we put that information aside. We would make a separate photocopy and put it in a folder. Some of it was -- and then having worked on this material for quite a period of time, one does become quite familiar with it, and then when you see new information, other documents or aerial images or whatever, it was possible to go back to that folder and to try to link things up independently from third sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you say "third sources," what sources are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I'm talking about documents, for example, that were seized from the VRS, documents that were received from the RS Ministry of Defence, documents -- notes that were taken by third parties, by UNPROFOR officers, aerial imagery, phone numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could the witness please be provided with Prosecutor's Exhibit 863, which is a binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, did you prepare Prosecutor's Exhibit 863?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was this exhibit or the materials that are contained in this exhibit collected during the time you were analysing these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you take Prosecutor's Exhibit 863, which should be before you, and could you describe to the Judges and to counsel the contents of this binder in general terms? Give them an orientation of what's in this binder.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Sure. The first page is an outline of the contents of the material. You'll see that there are 12 tabs. Each tab contains two summaries. The first summary contains -- the first is a summary of one or more intercepted conversations, and the second summary summarises the material that corroborates the intercept or intercepts that are contained in that tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, does this represent the totality of your work in this area or is this only a small sample of the documents, the intercepts, that you applied this process to?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That is a sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Could you kindly turn then to tab 1, to the first page in tab 1. Is that the summary of the intercepted telephone communication or communications that will be analysed against independent third-party information?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's take tab 1, and let's turn to the next page. There should be a summary, I'm sorry, an intercept dated the 11th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Judges then this process that you went through using this intercept as an example.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And tell the Judges, please, what these colours mean and the numbers mean and the like.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Sure. Well, there are four features, I guess, of this intercept and of the corroborating material, and those are the date, the time, the parties who are conversing, and then 12 highlighted points in this conversation. I would like to turn to the corroborating material.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine. So the date is the 11th of July at 1800 hours, and this is a conversation between General Gvero and General Gobillard.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This represents the substance of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you turn then to the corroborating material.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's found after your summary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct. I think it would be helpful, I mean, if it's possible to look at both at the same time. I've taken the intercept out of the binder to do this, but in the corroborating material, the same four features are important, namely, the date, the time, the parties, and then 12 additional highlighted points. So in both conversations, both conversations are dated the 11th of July, 1995. The intercepted conversation was recorded at 1800 hours. The corroborating material notes a time of 1810, and the two people conversing are General Gvero and General Gobillard. With regard to the corroborating material, I should say that these are notes that were taken by General Gobillard's military assistant, a Major Fortin. You will see his name at the bottom of the second page. These were contemporaneous notes that he recorded from the UNPROFOR side at the same time that this conversation was taking place. So if we could just look at point 2, perhaps, and the highlighted section of point 2. I might just read through point 2 and point 3 and then the remaining, I guess, ten points are very similar in their content. So looking at OTP Exhibit 350/A, which is the intercepted conversation, point 2 says: "It is now clear to me that General Gobillard gave the order for the shelling of the Serb positions. And that he still has those planes at his disposal, and it is his decision whether they will be used again." Point 2 on the corroborating material of Major Fortin's notes say: "General Gvero's first reaction was that it was now clear that it was General Gobillard who had called for the air power, who still had the aircraft at his disposal and who could still call for them." Point 3 of the intercepted material, OTP Exhibit 350/A, says, and this is General Gvero speaking: "If you and members have been shot at, it was not by us. Rather, following the familiar scenario, they were shot at by the Muslims, who are very close to them and whom you are protecting. Our troops didn't open fire on the UN, because the UN has never been, and I hope never will be, our enemy." Point 3 of Major Fortin's notes state: "If UNPROFOR troops were really targeted, then it was by the BiH, who fired onto them, according to their old scenario. Our army never attacked UNPROFOR, the BSA had never thought of UNPROFOR to be a belligerent party." The remaining highlighted points reflect such similarities between the two conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's turn now to tab 2. Can you take us through the exercise again?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Certainly. Here we have -- the date on these conversations is the 11th of July. There are five attached intercepts and they all make reference to a Serbian flag being placed on a Serbian Orthodox church in Srebrenica after VRS forces entered the town. The first -- the conversations recorded at 1655 and 1823 were recorded by the 2 Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a series of three conversations recorded at 1710 and shortly thereafter were intercepted by the State Security Service in Tuzla. So the first intercept was recorded at 1655 in the afternoon, and it's a conversation between participants "X" and "Y," meaning that they were unknown. The last time that "X" speaks - I believe the passage should be highlighted - it says: "Pass on a message to your command that there is a Serbian flag on the ruined Orthodox church in Srebrenica." Then the next page, which is OTP Exhibit 349/A, was also recorded on the 11th of July, at 1710 hours. It's a conversation between someone named Stankovic and an unidentified man designated as "X." The second time that "S," Stankovic, speaks, he says: "Listen. Just tell him there is a Serbian flag on the Serbian church in Srebrenica." Then on this same page, in another conversation, it states: "Right after this," meaning the previous conversation, "Stankovic talked to a man called Dusko." And in the first comment that "S," Stankovic, makes, he says: "You probably heard, but just for your information, the Serbian flag is fluttering on the Serbian church in Serbian Srebrenica." Then "D," Dusko, is inaudible. And then "S" says: "But listen, it's fluttering on the Serbian church in Serbian Srebrenica." Then moving down on that page, it states: "Right after this, Stankovic called a man named Garic. " And the second time that Stankovic speaks, he says: "Listen, you've probably heard, the Serbian flag is fluttering on the Serbian church in Serbian Srebrenica." The next and the last intercept in this series was recorded at 1823. It's between participants X and Y. And the third time that Y speaks, which is halfway down in the conversation, he says: "We called ... the whole town. Our flag is on the church ... the whole town. They are ..." The corroborating material for the previous intercepts are photographs that were extracted from video footage shot on both the 11th of July and the 13th of July. The reason that I included the material from the 13th of July is that there was a better still photograph that could be taken of the flag. So the first two exhibits that were extracted from OTP Exhibit 3, you'll see the Serbian church in Srebrenica on the hill, and on the next page you'll see a close-up of the flag on that church.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to tab 3, and could you -- do you have something else to say on this? I'm sorry. I've interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's okay. There's still actually two more photographs I'd just like to show, and these were taken on the 13th of July by a Serbian reporter, Zoran Petrovic. Again, it shows the same church on the first photograph, and on the second photograph it's a close-up of the flag, in which you can see the cross in the middle which would have had four inverted Cs around it, the Serbian flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention, please, to tab 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting you, Mr. Harmon, but I think that we've already understood what you are trying to do, the message you are sending to the Chamber, that is, the procedure that you utilised. I think that we have already understood that, so I don't think, unless the contents are important for you -- but as far as the Chamber is concerned -- I don't know what the position of my colleagues is, but I have understood the procedure. I don't know if it's the same thing for the Defence. So do we really have to go through the entire file? Because if we do, we're going to need a lot of time to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No. If the Court doesn't desire it, I'm perfectly happy to move on to a different subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that would be preferable, yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, at the conclusion of this exercise, Ms. Frease, did this exercise contribute to your satisfaction that the intercepts were genuine and they were reliable?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: During the whole period of time you were analysing these intercepts, did you find any evidence whatsoever that these intercepts were fabrications, were montages, were phonies?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your opinion, based on your work in this area of analysing these intercepts, what is your opinion as to whether or not these intercepts that you analysed and that have been tendered by the Prosecutor in this case are reliable?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I believe they're absolutely reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to a different topic, and if the Judges could have before them - I believe they may already - two exhibits that have been previously marked, Office of the Prosecutor Exhibit 364/1 and 2, and if I direct your attention to 364/2, which is similar in what we're going to be talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, in the course of your analysis of these intercepts, was part of your project to attempt to date, with specificity, the intercepts that you were analysing?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. That was a big part of the project.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you prepare the two exhibits that are now before you, Prosecutor's Exhibit 364, volume 1, and 364, volume 2?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There's an index contained in each of these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: These exhibits are dated. There's a tab with a date. And a number of exhibits, for example, that fall under the 15th of July have been identified, and then the 16th of July and the 17th of July, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let's focus first of all on the index. Did you prepare this index?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You'll see in the second column of the index there is a date attributed to each intercept that is contained in the binder.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could we take a look at, first of all, two intercepts. Are there changes that should be made in this index?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Could you just direct the Judges to those changes, and then I will ask you about them.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Uh-huh. It was something that we started from the beginning. When we received the first material, the printouts, many of the printouts were being translated, but at the same time we were entering them into a table, and many of the printouts that we received from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have dates on every page. So where we had a date that was firm, we would bold it so that we knew without question that that took place on that date. Where we didn't have a firm date typed on a page, then we would speculate as to the date in terms of where it came in the sequence, but we would not bold it, and that way we knew what was a firm date and what was not a firm date. When we received the notebooks, we went through a similar process, but the notebooks were much more helpful in dating the material. So where we found a date -- and I should say that we really focused initially, because of the volume of material and the few number of people who were working on the project, that we prioritised it and worked on roughly a ten-day period initially and then expanded that out. When we found a date handwritten into a notebook, we again knew that -- considered that to be a firm date and would indicate it as such, and were very diligence about keeping track of the dates. So the easy case was when we had a firm date in a notebook or on a printout. What was more difficult to figure out was when we had a range, for example, a date, a firm date of, say, the 12th of July written in a notebook and no dates for a number of days and then a date of the 16th of July. So we would go through the process. Since these were recorded chronologically, from the morning to the evening, in most cases, where it changed over from night to morning, we considered that to be the beginning of a new day. And if all of those matched up in the middle, from the 12th to the 16th, then we considered all of the dates in between to also be firm -- confirmed dates. Now, there was another way that we were able to date some of the conversations in the notebooks where we found overlapping conversations, where we knew that these were definitely the same conversation but had been recorded two or sometimes three times by different operators. If we had a confirmed date in one of the notebooks or two of the notebooks, then we also considered the date to be firm on that third conversation and then sometimes that would help us date the conversations as well. Additionally, when we received information from the SDB in Tuzla, their dating system was very strong on their printouts, and we also used that to corroborate the dates that we had. So dating, I would say, was an extremely important part of the process and something that we paid a lot of attention to.
