utterances.text: Again, I would have to refer to the entire body of the -- of my work, which I don't have here in front of me. I'd be happy to double-check it. I mean it's clear that on this page that date is indicated, I believe, but I would like to seen the original notebook as 10/8/1995, so the 10th of August, 1995. What makes me a little -- what makes me uncertain is that three -- let's see. About three pages prior to that, on page 00801928, there is a date of 19/9/1995, and on the subsequent -- on -- about three pages from that, there is another date on page 00801941, which indicates the 27th of October, 1995. So I would -- I mean clearly this falls out of a sequence. The other -- I believe I saw another date. Yes, I see another date further down in the notebook, on page 00801948, indicating the 31st of October, 1995. My --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, may I try and assist you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On page 1928, there is indeed the date 19th of September, as you said. On page 1934 that follows that page, there is the date the 10th of August, which is absolutely illogical --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: -- as the notebook is filled in in order. Immediately after that on that same page, if you look at the same conversation, you will find the date the 11th or the 14th of October, 1995. That is the first following conversation. The same page, 1934, a few lines later on, you have another date indicated.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Okay. Uh-huh. Yes. I expect that what happened was that the 10 and the 8 for the months were transposed, that in fact the first date that appears on page 00801934 should be the 8th of October, 1995. That would make sense with the sequence that we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In any event, there is a probability that this conversation took place in October. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the usher to show the witness Prosecution Exhibit 843 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, in your examination-in-chief, you told us that in the -- you worked in the OTP until July 2000.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I think that the evidence was obtained by the OTP a little later. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you to apply the same method you applied when you collected the corroborating material for one particular conversation, and that conversation is on page 01077815.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The conversation took place on channel -- I think it says number 2, at 1051.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: To me it looks like channel 5, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Possibly, yes. I have a poor copy. The conversation was between X and Y, and they are Bogicevic and General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: X: Hello. Y: Hello. X: Is Zivanovic there? Y: Yes, he is. Who wants him? X: Ah, Bogicevic from Belgrade. Y: Just a moment, please. X: Good day ... Just a moment, General, sir. Bogicevic is calling for you. Yes. Zivanovic: Yes. Bogicevic: Hello, Zile [phoen]. Zivanovic: Hi, Bogi. Bogicevic: Good luck. Zivanovic: Thank you. Bogicevic: I brought the truck ... 5 tonnes of goods you have here in Ljubovija. Zivanovic: Yes. That's just the same as if you were in Belgrade. Bogicevic: Well, what can we do now? That's what Triso told me. Zivanovic: What? Bogicevic: Triso told me to do that. Zivanovic: Triso doesn't understand anything about borders. Bogicevic: Yes. Zivanovic: If he told you, then inform him and give it to him. Bogicevic: We're going to take some over there up to you. Zivanovic: Where? Bogicevic: Over there where you are. Zivanovic: I'm in Belgrade now. Bogicevic: Uh-huh. Zivanovic: I liberated Srebrenica, and I have now been assigned a new duty. Bogicevic: Yes, yes. Okay. Zivanovic: How are you? Bogicevic: All right. Bogicevic, that is. Excellent. I'll come up there. Zivanovic: ... I'm not going anywhere. Bogicevic: I'll come up there now with some watermelons to help you cool down. Zivanovic: Okay. Bogicevic: Uh-huh. Zivanovic: How are my Serbian people doing? Bogicevic: All right. (Krile?) mine. Zivanovic: Everything's all right ... Say hello to the Serbs. Bogicevic: I will ... We'll be hearing each other. Zivanovic: Okay. Bogicevic: Bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, I did not interrupt you, but I think that you have already read this transcript for the LiveNote and I have remembered the date. I know the date. I'm not going to say the date because I don't want to influence the witness, but that was a repetition of the reading of that particular portion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that is correct, but I now have two questions to ask the witness. One is with respect to the date. The second is with respect to the contents, so I had to read it out again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, did you tell us the date, determine the date, although a witness has already done that. A Prosecution witness has already done that, but could you now determine the date of that conversation for us, please, again?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I think it is page 10 -- no, 0107798. I think it says the 14th of July, 1995 on that particular page. Perhaps we can begin ...

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: The number I thought you referred to was 01077794; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me help you. I'm going to read the last three digits of the page. 807. And on that page we have the conversation which took place at 2038 between General Zivanovic and Major Jokic, and in what we received from the Prosecution, it was taken on the 14th of July, in the evening, at, as I say, 2038 hours.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Okay. Right. And then there's another date, the date of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Then we have another date, yes. And on page 811, and I'm quoting the last digits, we have the 15th of July, 1995. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Following on from that logic, when was this -- when did this conversation take place?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher to prepare Prosecution Exhibit OTP 469 next, please, if he would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, we have the logics of it but not the answer. We haven't heard an answer yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're waiting, Your Honour. I'm waiting for the answer too, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Okay. If you can wait just a minute until I finish. Thank you. Yes. Okay. I found a date of the 18th of July on page 01077846 and have counted one, two days back. So 17, 16, this one dated on the 15th. So -- I'm afraid I'm going to have to ask you for the original number of the conversation we were looking at again. But it -- uh-huh. Yes. It would have been on the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, in this conversation, if you still have it in front of you, I'm going to quote a sentence. I'm going to quote one sentence from that conversation.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Please, if I could just turn back to it. Could you give me the number again?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In the second half of the conversation, at one point General Zivanovic says the following: "I have liberated Srebrenica, and I have now been given a new assignment." Ms. Frease, you have in front of you a document, a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 469. Yes, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Number 469. Could you turn to page 2 of the document. The first page is the accompanying letter for the documentation which the Government of Republika Srpska sent to the Tribunal, and page 2 is the decree of the president of the Republika Srpska of the 15th of July, 1995, by which Zivanovic is placed at their disposal, Milenko Zivanovic. Ms. Frease, my question is: Does this document confirm the sentence "I have now been given a new assignment," and is it the same document you yourself used in preparing the documents for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: To my -- the system that I used was to take in all of the relevant material that I could collect and to look at that, all of that material, for specific intercepts and to see whether there were any internal discrepancies among the documents that -- among the corroborating material that I would use, with internal inconsistencies based on a whole set of documents -- I mean, I guess a little bit of difficulty that I'm having is that I'm aware of some other information that might not support this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, let us put the question another way. Is there any consistency between this particular conversation and the document? You can give us a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I would like to read the intercept again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the original. Perhaps the original would assist the witness. I'm not sure how clear a copy she has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe that would be clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: While you're looking for it, Ms. Frease, may I --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It's not the same notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: May I put the question to you in another way? Does this document correspond to -- fit into the contents of the conversation? Does it fit into the contents and substance of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, the Defence has no further questions for this witness. Thank you, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well. I think this is a good time to take a break. I think that Mr. Harmon will also have an opportunity to look at the transcript during the lunch break, and then we can come back for any additional questions. I think we all need a break at this point, so let us take a 50-minute lunch break. We'll adjourn for lunch. Is that a sufficient time for you, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, how about you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes, but I would just like to take advantage of this opportunity to clarify one point. Ms. Frease, is she here as a witness or as an expert? Bearing in mind what she is doing in the Office of the Prosecution, do we treat her as a witness or in the same way that we treated expert witnesses? That is my question to Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can go right to the point. I will not have any contact with Ms. Frease between now and the time she resumes the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you have understood the sense of that question. We adjourn for 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. Visnjic on his feet. I suppose that you are going to communicate to us the result of the homework that you've been doing. [In English] Not that you've been doing, but the witness has done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I know that I said that I completed, but I would like to beg the Court's indulgence. I have just a brief area. So would the Trial Chamber allow me to ask a few more questions, and I promise they won't be more than three or four minutes. I omitted to bring up this topic, bogged up as we were by all the documents and material. I have asked Mr. Harmon, so perhaps he can give you his view on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, we see that the lunch hour is always very productive and fertile. Mr. Harmon, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was going to ask you, "What lunch hour?" Your Honour, but I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know that you have a very difficult and complicated lunch hour. But Mr. Visnjic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I shall do my best not to abuse the trust you have placed in me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, when did you learn for the first time of the alleged statement of General Krstic, which is mentioned here under the "Kill them all" statement?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Could you restate your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, the Prosecution has offered the Court a tape and notebooks, with a conversation which allegedly took place between General Krstic -- with General Krstic, and which internally -- or which we have become accustomed to calling, between the Defence and the Prosecution, the "Kill them all" conversation or statement. I think you are aware of the conversation I'm referring to. Now, when did you learn of that conversation first? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I believe that it was in the spring of 1999. I can't tell you the exact month, but probably April, May, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What was your reaction when you heard about that conversation for the first time, that is to say, when you analysed the conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, the first reaction was one of some surprise because it was new to us. We first heard it on tape and had not come across it in any of the written material.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you came across it in the written material. And when was that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That was shortly thereafter. Because we hadn't heard it in the material before, I thought that it must not have taken place in July, since most of the material that we had covered -- since the material that we covered focused on July. So I went through notebooks, I identified notebooks that contained transcribed conversations from August, and I began to look through them, and that was how I found the written notebook, and it was shortly after hearing the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you consider that to be significant evidence, one of the most important for the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Because there were a lot of conversations that were important.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What efforts did you make to identify the voice of General Krstic on that tape, and were you at all able to -- were you at all involved in those activities?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Not in any sort of formal way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I object to that question. We've presented to the Chamber an expert witness that represents our efforts to identify the voice - the Court has heard that witness, Dr. French - and they've heard another witness, whose name I will not reveal, also in respect of that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will withdraw my question and rephrase it. Mr. President, I'll withdraw the question and go on to my next question, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Excuse me, please, Mr. Visnjic. I myself have a question. Did you hear several diskettes or reels?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many times, more or less, did you hear the voice of -- no. Let me rephrase that. Did you identify the voice of General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you recognise a voice which was could supposedly have been that of General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I could not recognise General Krstic's voice independent without there having been reference made within a particular transcript or -- right, within a tape recording or a transcript of who the conversants were. A main part of my job did not involve listening to the conversations. That work was primarily carried out by the language assistants, interpreters, translators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well. Mr. Visnjic, you may proceed. Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, perhaps I should have put my question a different way. What efforts did the Prosecution take in the sense of confirming identification? But Mr. Harmon has already answered that question, and I just wish to clarify what I meant in asking that question. Now, my following question is: Did you ask the people who conducted the intercepts about this particular conversation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Was that the interview with Witness Z of the 21st of November, 1999, or sometime in that period?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I believe I know who you're referring to. It would make me more comfortable to see the name of Witness Z, but I did conduct a conversation with one witness regarding that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you remember whether it was in the autumn of 1999?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know why this conversation was not used in the main part of the Prosecution presentation of evidence?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Why was this conversation not included into the evidence that you prepared, and that is Exhibit 364 that you prepared for the main part of the presentation of the Prosecution's evidence?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I was asked to prepare those binders, which is what I did. It was a process that we went through. The final decision about all of the documents that were included was not my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Harmon, we are now going to see how productive exactly your lunch break was. Any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I do have some.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn first of all, Ms. Frease --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The witness should be provided with Prosecution Exhibits 364/1 and 364/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have those in front of you, Ms. Frease?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were asked about a conversation that is found in Volume 1 at July 13th, tab 14. Would you turn to that tab, please. This is a conversation that is intercepted at 2010 hours on channel 5B, bottom code-name. It starts at the top with that.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have that conversation in front of you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The question my that colleague Mr. Visnjic asked you was was this conversation confirmed or corroborated, and what I would like to do, please, is I'd like to go through this conversation in light of the knowledge of your events of what occurred in Srebrenica and ask you to, first of all, direct your attention to the first reference to the gentleman named Deronjic. Who do you believe that to be?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I believe that to be a gentleman by the name of Miroslav Deronjic, from Bratunac, who at the time had been appointed as the civilian commissioner to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And indeed, this conversation deals with civilians, in part, does it not; or Muslims, in part, does it not?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, independently, are you aware that Miroslav Deronjic was in fact in Bratunac on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you aware of that based on film that you have seen of negotiations -- I'll take that back. Strike that. How are you aware that Mr. Deronjic was in Bratunac on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Through film footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is it also -- actually, let me then ask you to go to the next area where it says: [As read] "Deronjic: The president is asking how many thousands," and the next reference is: "About 2.000 for the time being." On the 13th of July, are you aware that there were Muslim prisoners being detained in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And is the figure, the reference that's made in this intercept that there were at least "2.000 for the time being" consistent with your knowledge of the events on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I can't put a number to the number of people who were detained, but I am aware that many Muslims were detained in Bratunac on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you -- then go down to the bottom, two sets, where it says: "Deronjic: The president says all the goods must be placed inside the warehouses before 12.00 tomorrow." The next line: "Deronjic: Right. Deronjic: Not in the warehouses but somewhere else." Are you aware that on the 13th of July, Muslim prisoners who were being detained in Bratunac were moved from Bratunac to locations elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And where were those individuals moved in?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: They were primarily moved to schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What location? Outside of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Outside of Bratunac, yes. In the Zvornik municipality in general, and also, I guess, Pilica is -- well, that was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Therefore, in looking at this intercept, when my colleague asked you if this conversation has been corroborated, are there elements contained in this conversation that have been corroborated by independent investigation conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: The information in here is consistent with what we have found in the investigation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Let me turn now to Volume 2, if I could, and refer you to in the last conversation, a conversation dated the 2nd of August. Do you have that conversation in front of you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this is a conversation that has a telephone number in it; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you said on your direct examination that one of the ways that you considered attempting to verify whether or not these documents were genuine was by consulting a number of sources, including telephone books; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the Prosecutor's Exhibit 863 that has been shown to you earlier and that you prepared, there is in fact one tabbed item where there's a reference to a telephone book; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of whose telephone number is mentioned in this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It appears to be General Krstic's telephone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you aware that General Krstic, on the 1st of November, 2000, when asked by my colleague, Mr. McCloskey, about whose telephone number that was, confirmed indeed that that was his telephone number?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And that, for Your Honours' reference, is found at pages 6814 and 6815 of the Prosecutor's - I'm sorry - of the English language version of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let's examine this just a little bit further. You're unfamiliar, according to your testimony, with somebody, an officer, by the name of Delgadasi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But General Krstic in his cross-examination has confirmed the telephone number that is contained in this particular intercept, this being his own.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is that a factor that -- how do you weigh that factor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I would consider that -- I would consider it very strong corroborating material for this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to another item that was referred to by my colleague, and it is found in OTP Exhibit 289.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I don't have that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could that exhibit, please, be furnished to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the conversation I'm directing your attention to is found at the page that has the ERN number with the last four digits 1429.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this is a conversation -- actually, I'll withdraw that question. Can you date this conversation? Are you able to date this conversation by looking at any other notes that you may have?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: The material that I wanted to obtain during lunchtime is voluminous and hasn't been printed out, so I'll just try to look at the notebook and see if I can find a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, if you go to 1416 --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if you go to 1438 --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- you will see two dates.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And just, then, if you don't have your other materials based on at least your preliminary analysis of comparing the dates and the location of the conversation in respect of those dates, are you able to give us at least a tentative answer as to when this conversation occurred?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. On the 25th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, were events occurring in Zepa on the 25th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were civilians who were in Zepa being evacuated by bus?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can't read the language, but I have obtained a copy of the LiveNote, and I'd like to read you a portion of what has been interpreted in the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, perhaps for the benefit of the Defence, you could give us the page number, and for our benefit as well, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me -- unfortunately, I can't read this, but I have the translation. I can direct my colleagues, perhaps, to the sentence and they can find it in the -- I think it will be actually -- actually, I believe it will be on page with the last four digits 1430.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There's a reference to -- it's been translated as follows. One of the correspondents says, [As read] "Literally, that we behave in a civilised manner and that all men behave in that way so that we don't -- that we shouldn't have a repetition of the problems we had before." Now, by the 25th of July, 1995, had it, as far as you're aware, come to the attention of the media and the world's attention that there had been, allegedly, large-scale killings of Muslim prisoners and Muslim civilians in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, by the 25th of July, was that -- were the people in the VRS aware that the world was now focusing on the events related to the takeover of the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, then the sentence that I've just read to you, that "We should behave in a civilised manner so we don't have a repetition of the problems we had before," in light of the events, the date, are you able to give us any view at all as to what this may refer to?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. Am I also able to draw upon other material that I remember reading in the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, I recall a conversation in which a VRS Main Staff officer, I believe, mentioned it was -- it was a similar conversation, but at a higher level, and there was an order given to the effect -- the line was, "Not a single hair must be missing from their heads," something to that effect, that the impression from that conversation, this conversation, and others, was that there was -- actually, that also the officers were to be dressed well along the road, the VRS officers were to be dressed well, they were to behave well, because there was going to be press, as I recall, but certainly international monitors observing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember any intercepts at all dealing with -- about CNN paying attention to these events, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I don't. I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. I have no additional questions, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Judge Fouad Riad, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have just a general question to start with concerning what you call the labourious process to deal with the material. Now, when you have to question or to verify that the document, a tape, has to meet with certain requirements of reliability, and these requirements are not fulfilled, do you discard it completely or do you still keep it in case of doubt?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Are you referring specifically to -- are you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. Suppose, for instance, you have a tape where the voice is not clear or where the names are not mentioned, and you gave us several tests. You said you have to -- the intercepts should be consistent with what you knew about the case and with other -- with information coming from other sites, and there should be no internal -- there should be not be -- there should be no internal inconsistencies and so on. In case of -- if there is an internal inconsistency or difficulty to, let us say, to compare and so on, do you still maintain the document or the tape?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely. We listened to everything, we analysed everything, we read everything. And, you know, especially at the beginning, but even throughout the process, there were times that we didn't understand what we were hearing or what we were reading, that there was just something that was new to us that would come up. Everything was processed -- the material was processed in the same systematic pattern. We didn't make any judgements about the content of the material; we just processed it all. And then, of course, as the investigation continued and as we learned more, sometimes what might have seemed to be irrelevant at one moment made sense in the light of other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: There, in fact, the final decision of all the documents - I'm quoting you - the final decision of all the documents that were included was not your own, but were you still seriously involved in assessing, in the assessment of the documents?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you could -- you could eliminate what was not up to the standard after awhile?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It wasn't necessarily what wasn't up to the standard. It was -- I mean we included -- as I said, we included everything. So I'm not quite clear what ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Why did you mention that you have got several factors in assessing the reliability? If these factors are not met with, what do you do?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I'm still not sure that I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You have to verify the reliability or not?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, as an entire -- as an entire set, for example, first we used the printouts. Those were the documents that we were given first by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were some 500 and -- almost 600 pages. On each page there would have been mostly more than one -- more than one conversation, sometimes several conversations. So we went through that entire process of entering those within a specific date range. Actually, all of those were entered because they were within July of 1995. Then we went back to the notebooks and we started processing the notebooks. From the notebooks then, we tried to match the notebooks up to the conversations that we had already entered into our database and got matches. And so every time we had a verbatim match of a document, a printed document of what the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina said was -- what they told us had been transcribed, when we found it with the notebook, then we would match those up. Additionally, when we received the material from the state security service in Tuzla, we went through the same process of matching up conversations again. Then when -- so there could conceivably be, say, a couple of matches internally between printouts and notebooks and possibly, but in few cases, tapes. Then as we continued the process of analysis, we came across conversations that were clearly the same conversation. In some cases, we could verify that because it was the same date, but the times were very similar. Not to the minute, but usually within five minutes. So then we took those conversations and by running through the database again, we would then link those conversations with the newly found conversations, always working to match all of the information back together. There was some material that we weren't able to -- that we didn't find -- that we didn't have both printouts and notebooks for, but that was, you know, always indicated as such in our records. And the dates, also I mentioned that on the dates we were very -- I think very diligent in ensuring that the dates were firm. Where we could confirm the dates, we always noted that; and where we could not confirm the dates, we always noted that as well. Then over time and continuing through this process, we were, in many cases, able to confirm dates through the other documents, either through receiving the notebooks or receiving material from the CSB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I understood that was your process. Now you have to wait, of course, until you identify it. You categorise, let's say, the reliability of your documents after that? You say this is the first class reliable. The other one is -- in case of doubt, you continue on searching and so on, and if you do not find any consistency, you just rule it out?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- after awhile?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No. The database contains all of the information. There was never anything that was eliminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. Now, would you take anything on its face value? For instance, in a tape, an intercept, they say, for instance, "I am Mr. So-and-so talking to you. " Would you take that for granted or you tried to verify if it corresponds to the truth?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: This is where speaking with the intercept operators was very helpful. Excuse me. They -- we had questions about that, but we noticed that in looking at the material, if a person's name was mentioned in the conversation, if one person addressed another person by their name or by their rank or in some way, then -- this depended a little bit on the operators, but generally what they would do is in the heading where you have the participants they might say "X" but put the person's name in parentheses. I'm hesitating a little bit, because in other cases I believe, and now it's been many months, almost a year since I've been doing this, but I believe they might have written the name. If they got the name from the conversation as a person directing a comment to someone else by their name, then they would have written that name up in the header of that conversation, and this is what we noticed. This is what I noticed from the work that we conducted as well. If there was ever any doubt as to who was speaking, there was absolute consistency in putting X and Y. The other time that people -- that an operator might put a name in parentheses is if he recognised the name. Because the operators listened and got to know people's voices, they would never indicate that as a firm identification, but they might indicate that the speaker could be a particular person through voice recognition, and that would be designated in parentheses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: May I just ask a peripheral question. Before coming to the OTP, were you involved in the same kind of work?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because you have a Master's Degree from the School of International Affairs.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's a school where I was a professor. We did not used to teach this kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So what experience did you have before that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have any experience in dealing with intercepted communications, certainly. My background is in international affairs, and I worked in the field in the former Yugoslavia for a couple of years during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad, and especially for your testimony too. Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, just a couple of questions. One I think you may have answered, but I just have to get it in the right context. In the beginning, you said you translated the majority of intercepts, mostly in terms of the time frame that you were especially interested in, that week or two weeks in July. Why -- is it true that there were some in those weeks that you didn't translate, and if so, why not?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: We translated -- when we first received the material in March of 1998 - that's the printout material - we translated everything, all of the pages, every conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, when you were translating all the conversations, and you said you put them all into the database, but then you also told us that you kept sort of corroborating files like the one that you showed us, for some or all, or how did you pick the ones that you kept corroborating files? Just that you happened to come upon corroboration?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No. It was mostly based on the content of the conversation, whether it appeared as if a particular piece of information within that conversation seemed as if it was something that we might be able to corroborate, like phone numbers or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. When you came upon particular conversations, some might immediately, I assume, stand out in your own mind or anyone else's as being important. In fact, you said that one reason that you didn't consider the "Kill them all," one to be as important as others, I think is what you said, but when you found those ones you did think were important, did you have any system for immediately bringing them to the attention of the people on the investigative task force or did you -- at what point did those corroborating notebooks or your own feeling that something was important get put into the process?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: There wasn't a system per se, but we spoke every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So in other words, if you came upon something that you thought was really hot stuff, then you would communicate with somebody in the task force.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you ended up having files for some -- corroborating files for some but not for others; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did you have a corroborating file for the "Kill them all"?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you didn't think that was even important enough or you didn't come across any corroboration?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: One or both of the answers I proffered.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right. That conversation didn't seem to contain anything that we could corroborate independently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: There were a lot of specifics in it. It was past the two weeks that you said you concentrated on, but there were a lot of specific things in there. You said that you found it not as important as other conversations that you came across in the intercepts. Can you, offhand, remember any one you can cite to us that's already in evidence that you would have said was more important?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I think and I hope I said that I didn't consider it to be more -- necessarily more important than other conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You just said, I think -- I don't have your quote, but the impression left with me is you didn't think it was a top-level, important conversation. You used the phrase: "There were others that were more important."

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Okay. I mean for me it fit within a sort of bundle of conversations that were important. I can -- I can remember a few of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, even one or two, just so I get --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Sure. The 16th of July conversation in which at 1358 in the afternoon, I think it was, in which 500 litres of D2 fuel were being ordered to Pilica village, Lieutenant Colonel Popovic. There were the conversations between -- on the 15th of July between Colonel Beara and General Krstic which I considered to be important. There were a couple of conversations later. There was one conversation later in the day, I think at 2116 on the 16th, in which Lieutenant Colonel Popovic tries to report back to General Krstic, who is unavailable, and therefore leaves him a message that the work has been done or that the job is finished, I think were the words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So is this a correct impression I'm getting, that is, you were looking through -- you were interested in kind of down-to-earth, possibly, factual proof of events that went on on particular days so that when you hit an excerpt which said "Kill them all," even though some might say that that had import in terms of attitude, intent, that sort of thing, you didn't think that was as important?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: You know, one thing that I thought was that it could have just been military talk, people in the field. I mean I'm not in the military. I've then been in the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But you must have heard a lot of military intercepts in your work. Okay. So in other words, just to get rid of that particular -- you didn't do any prioritising of that in terms of you didn't report that immediately to one of your investigative teammates and say, "Hey, we've got kind of an important one here. You should listen and take care of it"?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No. I mean we reported it right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, I mean you put it in the database, I know, but you didn't single it out for any kind of special attention or you did?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, yes. We talked about it because it wasn't -- I mean, what was unusual about it was, you know, the specific content of that conversation. So, yes, we talked about it right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. On a more general topic, you told us that your corroboration file or you would try to put together in a file sometimes things that corroborated stuff that was in the intercept itself and then sometimes you would evaluate the intercept in terms of "Whether it was consistent with what we knew about the case." Now, did you -- my first question is: In your experience, did you or the people that were working for you ever come across intercepts which were not consistent with what you knew about the case, and if so, what would you do about them? Would you make a note? Would you tell your investigative fellow teams, "Hey, maybe you ought to be careful about this one because it doesn't seem to gel with some other stuff that we've got"?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I never felt that there were any inconsistencies within the material. There were certainly things that we didn't understand within the material, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But in all these intercepts, you never found any one that you thought: Gee, this is odd. It just doesn't seem to gel with what we know about what else is going on?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Were you -- when I asked you before, you know, you were on the alert, obviously, for communications which would provide evidence of what the team was investigating. What about if you came across something, and did you ever come across something, that went the other way, I mean, that seemed to be, if anything, exculpatory?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes what?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Well, I mean, there were some things -- for example, there was earlier mention of where -- of General Zivanovic's whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: And that was something that, you know, was sort of -- that we weren't -- we didn't quite know how to place for, you know, for some time. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Would you discuss that? If you came across something and you thought: Gee, you know, this --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You would go to your mates --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: -- your mates, and you'd say, "Well, gee, you better be aware that there's this around --"

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So did -- my last question: Did you at some point -- you were keeping -- you were putting everything in the database, you were occasionally talking to your -- well, maybe more than occasionally talking to your investigative mates about things that particularly aroused your attention, good or bad, as they came through the process. Now, at the end of the process, when decisions were being made, I guess, about what evidence might be culled for the proceeding, did they ever come back to you? I mean, what did you do with your corroborative files as they moved along? Say you had an intercept on day one, you put it into the file -- into the database; as time went on, you found collaborating evidence coming in, you kept a file on that, evidence coming in. At some point did you input that cumulating knowledge back into the investigative team so they could help evaluate the intercept, in light of what you knew about it? They might know about it, but they might not know all the same things you knew about it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: It's a very complicated question. You put the material in the database as you translated it, you kept an ongoing corroborative file so that if new information came which might have corroborated that, it went into your corroborative file; right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No. Actually, it was that we would keep -- the file consisted of material within the intercepts that looked as if it might be possible to corroborate, and not the reverse, if I've understood you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. But even if, even if -- yes. Even if that's true, you would -- sometimes your file would develop as you went along. I mean, you would file some new -- find some new intercepts that corroborated the old ones or the telephone.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So did you ever, at the end of the process, after you had the corroboration files, go back to the team and give them the benefit of that corroboration so that they could put it into their evaluation of the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You just kept them, the corroboration file, on the shelf, or what?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, you see -- right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please pause before giving an answer to give the interpreter's a chance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: It's such a privilege for me to speak to somebody in my own language. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: This file was a little hanging file, and when we would find something, we would make a photocopy of it and just stick it in there. Doing -- you know, doing the third-party corroboration was not -- it was a part of the whole project, but relatively speaking, it was a very small part of the whole --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me just sum up in the final question. Did they, the other members of the investigative team - the investigators, the lawyers, whoever else who were going to finally put together the case, did they ever come back to you on the intercepts and say, "Well, we're planning to use certain intercepts. We want to ask you about certain ones" or once you'd gotten them into the database it was all done with, from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, I guess I helped to identify those that were most pertinent to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Judge Wald. You're really privileged, because you can speak your own language. I never have that chance. Ms. Frease, I too have a few questions for you. So at the beginning there was your project of intercepts, with certainly objectives in mind - organise the material, translate it, file it - and you had a series of resources to do it. You mentioned translators in the field. I must admit that I don't quite understand who those people were and what they did for your project. "Field translators," could you explain the concept, the notion, who they were?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Sure. We used them at the very beginning of the project, again in spring 1998, when we received the first printed material and were very eager -- the team was very eager to know what that material contained. So for the sake of expediency, I put together a small group of translators for -- twice - it might have been three times, but two or three times - a small group of translators who sat down in a room, and I was with them, and just started working through, from page 1 through page 564, I think. And so that material was translated in that way and provided the investigative team with an ability to begin to look at that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Another question. You mentioned, in connection with certain problems that you felt, you said two or three conversations which were not the same but which were recorded by different operators. Could you please explain a little the type of situation you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Certainly. There were -- the 15th of July there was a conversation between General Krstic and Colonel Beara, and that conversation was recorded, I believe, by three different operators. Each conversation varied slightly, but there were enough elements in those conversations to allow us to say with certainty that it was the same conversation but recorded by different operators and from at least two locations, from two locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how did that situation fit into your objective of corroborating the conversations or to make sure that they were consistent?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that there were three recordings of the same conversation but that there were slight differences between them; they were not exactly identical. The fact that they were not exactly the same, did that cause problems for you to be able to assess them regarding the validity of the conversation itself, the message it contained, the content?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: One conversation might provide more information, an additional name that another operator wasn't able to hear that someone else could hear. You know, what we were most interested in was just ensuring that we had matched everything up together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could it be said that at the end, the fact that they were not absolutely identical could prove to be a test of the content because one provided something that the other did not? Am I understanding you correctly, Ms. Frease? Very well. There's another question. You spoke about the State Security Service in Tuzla. You spoke about the SSB [as interpreted] in Tuzla. You also spoke about the SDB in Tuzla. I don't know what that is. It is on page 31, line 10 of the LiveNote. What are they? SDB, what is the SDB in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It's the State Security Service in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same thing?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It is. CSB generally refers to a larger area that might contain several SDBs, but yes, it's the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is one situation where three things apply to the same thing, tell us the same thing.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question for you. Not all the intercepts were translated. You focused basically on a time frame beginning the 10th of July. So the beginning was the 10th of July, and up to when?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: We did it in phases, because we weren't sure how long the process was going to take, and so that was a place where we did prioritise them. So approximately from the 10th of July to the 20th of July, but it might have even been the 10th to the 18th. I don't exactly remember. After we processed all of that material, then we expanded the whole process to include all of July, from the beginning of July through -- through the beginning of August, especially after, you know, after we discovered the conversation from the 2nd of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we try to establish a relationship between those dates and the indictment, how would you see it? If we compare the dates that you focused on and the indictment, what link could you establish, if there is any?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Could you tell me what you're referring to in the indictment? I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The indictment, as you know, mentions dates. There is a time, a time period when the facts occurred. So my question is whether the dates that you focused on have anything to do with the dates referred to in the indictment, the dates when the crimes were allegedly committed.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. We focused on -- as I said, July, but then for the situation of the reburials we looked at notebooks from that period of time to see whether there was anything obvious from that time period. But I don't recall -- we didn't -- you know, the analysts -- the language people who looked at those periods didn't find anything that appeared to be related.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Another question, and that will be the last. You had this lengthy experience with the processing of intercepts. You worked on the establishment of co-relations among documents and their corroboration, and if I were to ask you to fabricate a message like this one, "Kill them all," what would you do? How would you go about it, make a montage of such an intercept? I'm asking you to do that, and then I'm asking you how you would go about it.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's a -- well, I'd have to start back at the beginning with the typed records and with the notebooks, and I guess, you know -- I mean, you would have to fill an entire notebook with fabricated material. In terms of making a recording, I don't have any of that kind of background, so I really -- I -- I don't know how I would do it. I don't know how it would be done. Cutting and pasting, I guess, things together, but I -- it's not really the area that I -- it's not my area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in any event, you would have to de-codify a message. If you were to have to work in the opposite direction, how many persons or what kind of expertise would you need to do it? Or you don't even want to think about it? It wouldn't interest you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- I don't feel qualified to know how to do that, since I wasn't someone who was actually participating in the transcription, in the listening, in the recording, and all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But there is a possibility of you going back to your school and teaching these things. That is why Judge Riad has a question for you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, it is just an answer which you gave to the president which I would like to understand more and have the benefit of your experience. You mentioned, in particular, three conversations between General Krstic and Beara, and each conversation varied slightly from the other. Would that be considered as a sign of inconsistency or of authenticity? How would you take it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: As internal consistency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Internal consistency?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now then, in that case they should be the same as the same day, same hour?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Very close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What should you check typically because you said they are varied, they are different?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right, but usually off within a minute or two, a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The variation would be what, in words, in -- or just in the time, as you said?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It would be in the time but it would also be in the substance of the text, because depending on where the operators were recording, where they were listening from, sometimes one signal came in stronger than another signal. And so some people would hear one part of a conversation better than they would hear another conversation. And by putting these things together, you know, we could come up with a good idea of what the whole conversation was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So that's what you call the internal consistency?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right. I mean, knowing that -- having people, the same people identified, having the same subject matter discussed, on the same day, at the same time. But we were always extremely sure before we made these kinds of -- before we would confirm that it was the same conversation, we had to be absolutely sure that it was the same conversation, and never made a match that we were unsure about. If we were unsure about it, we didn't match it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Frease, you have just completed your testimony here. Thank you very much for your contribution, which has assisted us a great deal, both us, the Defence, and the Prosecution, and we wish you a safe journey home and success in your work. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, I think you have some documents that you wish to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. We would move for admission Prosecutor's Exhibit 863.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Defence. Mr. Visnjic, what is your comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Exhibit -- Prosecutor Exhibit 863 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Harmon, what next?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My next witness is Mr. Kruszewski, and for that, Mr. President, I would ask for a closed session. I will explain in this private session the reason why I'm making that request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move into private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 23rd day of March, 2001, at 9.20 a.m.
